note: Each family is a workload shape with a size knob and a DECLARED complexity class. `maximum_exponent` bounds the exponent of `y = a*x^b` fitted by linear regression on (log size, log inferences) across the whole ladder, so the family is held to its class rather than to a constant. `maximum_growth` is the factor any size may cost above its pinned row in scaling-baseline.json, which catches a constant-factor loss that leaves the class alone. `route`, where present, names the route every size must still be on; a size that left it is REFUSED rather than fitted, because a fallback silently changes what is being measured. Ladders are chosen so the classes are far apart: the sibling project's own note on the two quadratics that survived its kernel is that 'every one of these families is flat at the tens'.
counter_note: Inferences are deterministic and load-immune, so this gates on a shared workstation. Measured 2026-08-26: across three fresh processes per size, every one of the eight families returned the IDENTICAL count at every size, spread 0 absolute and 0 relative, and the same counts came back from a run at loadavg 3.40 and a run at loadavg 5.97. Repeating a call inside ONE process is not the same thing and is not what the gate does. Re-measured 2026-08-27 over five repeated calls at size 400: the six seeded families spread 0.0000% to 0.6556%, widest on chain-join, and in every one of them the FIRST call is the outlier and the rest are identical, so a loop measures a warm-up rather than a distribution. Worse, a workload that accumulates does not merely get noisier, it measures something else: planted-quadratic spreads 720.34% that way, because each repetition scans everything the previous one wrote. Repetitions are therefore processes. A family whose work crosses into C or Rust retires no inferences there, so it declares `paired_counter` and can be measured a second time under `perf stat -e instructions:u` with --paired; that second lane is ADVISORY and never gates, because this workstation is shared.
ported_from: metta-on-mork benchmarks/program-scaling-policy.json and scripts/check_program_scaling.py. What ported is the SCHEMA: a per-family `sizes` ladder, a declared bound on the growth exponent, and a SEPARATE looser bound on the constant factor against a recorded ledger. The SCRIPT did not, and neither did its numbers. Its counter is perf retired instructions where this lane's primary is inferences, which removes its CPU pinning (`performance_gate.pin_to`, hardcoded to cpu 11 where available) and its quiet-box requirement; it reaches into `check_direct_performance` for that pinning, source digests and cpu model, none of which have an equivalent here; its `BUDGET` and `NO_ROUTING=1` environment are kernel-specific; its refusal reads one `native_answered` field printed by one probe binary where a route here is per family and observed through the engine, because PeTTa's routes are per surface (`parser:petta_c_reader_active/0`, `seam:foreign_space/1`); and its constant guard compares `counts[-1]` alone where this one compares every size, since a curve that bends mid-ladder passes a last-size check. The ESTIMATOR is the reason its bounds cannot be reused: it takes the MAXIMUM of consecutive-pair slopes, this takes the regression exponent over all points. Recomputed on its own committed ledger on 2026-08-26, every one of its ten families reads LOWER under regression than under max-pair, by 0.008 to 0.235 (car_walk 1.542 -> 1.307, space_facts 0.515 -> 0.346, many_equations 0.474 -> 0.323), so adopting its numbers would have loosened every bound. The bounds here are set from this tree's own measurements instead. The two estimators agree to within 0.017 on the six seeded families below, which is what a ladder tall enough to reach the asymptote looks like; the gap is 0.117 on planted-quadratic, because a quadratic still carrying a linear term settles more slowly, and it is widest on the sibling's families exactly where its ladders stop short.

families.name: write-door
families.detail: n separate writes into one space, which `add-single` pins at a single size and nothing measures across sizes. A write cost that starts depending on how much is already stored is the shape this catches.

families.name: parse-forms
families.detail: one program text holding n forms, parsed once. The coverage survey names the parser as one of four surfaces where a class regression is invisible today. It OBSERVES its route (`c` when engine/reader.so loaded, `prolog` otherwise) but does not pin a value, because the two routes are both shipped: check.sh builds reader.so where swipl-ld exists and prints a note and gates the Prolog reader where it does not, and PETTA_C_READER=off selects the fallback deliberately. Pinning `c` here would make this lane red on a box the rest of the gate accepts, and both routes hold the SAME class, which is what makes not pinning it safe: measured 2026-08-27 on this family's own ladder, the Prolog route fits exponent 1.010 against the C route's 0.998, so the declared class catches a quadratic on either box. What the route changes is the CONSTANT, and it changes it by a lot: [55248, 111250, 223254, 452062] against [5222, 10422, 20822, 41624], a ratio of 10.58 to 10.86 across the four sizes. Against the 1.1 growth bound the guard would certainly fire, and that is the problem rather than the protection: it would name a parser regression where nothing regressed and only the box differs. So the configuration stamp refuses FIRST, the way BenchmarkBaseline.observe_configuration already refuses a drifted comparison for baseline.json, and it names the remedy. Verified end to end: PETTA_C_READER=off makes this lane print `CONFIGURATION DRIFT c_reader: pinned under True, measuring under False` and exit 1 before it fits anything. The route also has to hold across the whole ladder within a single run, which catches a fallback that happens mid-run.

families.name: chain-join
families.surface: the join planner: a conjunctive match with a shared variable
families.detail: two patterns joined on a shared variable over a path of n edges. The path keeps the ANSWER count linear, so the class is the finding rather than the output size: an unindexed nested-loop join is quadratic here and an indexed one is linear. This is the family most likely to hide a quadratic, because the engine's own note records that a conjunctive match IS a nested-loop join and is quadratic under skew.

families.name: selective-query
families.surface: the matcher: one selective lookup against a space of n facts
families.detail: declared CONSTANT, which is the strongest statement in the file. The moment a lookup stops reaching its index this becomes linear and the exponent gate says so, where a point pin at one size would see only a bigger number and read it as a constant-factor regression. The bound of 0.25 is well above the -0.013 measured and well below the 1.0 a lost index would produce.

families.name: segment-split
families.detail: two gaps around a separator splitting a row of n children. 896 lines with ZERO performance measurement at any layer, and split enumeration by backtracking is the classic quadratic, so this is where one would hide. The ladder stops at 800 because a flat row's children become a Prolog procedure arity and SWI refuses one above 1024.

families.name: mork-write
families.surface: the MORK backend write path, through seam:foreign_space/1
families.detail: n writes into a `&mork:` space. This family exists as much for its REFUSAL as for its curve: with the backend artefact absent the name silently becomes an ordinary native space, and the coverage survey records that two already-gated curves can therefore compare MORK pins against native measurements. Two fences stop that here, and both were demonstrated on 2026-08-27 by moving libmork_ffi.so aside. The configuration stamp refuses first, `mork_backend: pinned under 'foreign', measuring under 'native'`, exit 1. Underneath it, and reached by the --record path that skips the stamp check, the route check refuses all four sizes: `mork-write at size 200 took route 'native', not the declared 'foreign'`. What that prevents is concrete: the native space costs [5029, 10028, 20028, 40030] against this family's pinned [30010, 59897, 119899, 240505], so a missing backend would have read as a 6.0x improvement. Its growth bound is 1.10, the same as every other family: across fresh processes, which is what the gate measures, this family is exact like the rest, and inference count is Prolog-side and so cannot be loosened on the grounds that the work crosses into Rust. That blindness is what `paired_counter` is for.

families.name: planted-quadratic
families.surface: NEGATIVE CONTROL for the exponent gate
families.detail: the write-door workload with a full scan of the space added to every write, so a cost paid once per step grows with everything written so far. That is the exact shape of the two quadratics the sibling project found inside a lane whose own assertions were on charged steps. It is DECLARED linear, so the exponent gate has to catch it; measured 1.746 against the 1.25 bound. It is here permanently, the way Renaissance ships dummy-validation-failing, and the lane fails if it ever stops failing.

families.name: planted-constant-factor
families.surface: NEGATIVE CONTROL for the constant guard
families.detail: the write-door workload run three times over, pinned against the row for running it once. The class is untouched, so this must PASS the exponent gate at 0.999 and FAIL the growth gate at 2.99x, which is what proves the two gates are independent rather than one gate wearing two names. Its pinned row is write-door's own measurement and is never re-recorded: re-pinning it would replace the plant with its own inflated cost and the lane would go green having proved nothing.
